Guy Hall

Guy Hall  

Françoise, Dolto, child, France, castration, image, desire, verte

This paper serves as a brief introduction into the life and works of the French psychoanalyst, Françoise Dolto. Although acclaimed around the world, she is almost unknown in the United Kingdom as most of her books are not available in translation. It is suggested that this omission is largely due to the complicated post-war politics amongst Parisian psychoanalytic organizations and with the IPA. With reference to four questions, it is hoped that this paper will stimulate a greater interest into her life, her theoretical ideas and her clinical work, so that they become better known and her contribution to psychoanalysis can receive the recognition it deserves.

I was astonished to read an author's assertion, during an exercise to publicize her new book, that those who refuse to acknowledge the duality of the sexes are either ‘militant (female) homosexuals’ or ‘militant intersex’ (Chiland 2008, p. 14). For as long as I can remember, I have always, as a rather boringly straightforward heterosexual female, questioned these kinds of dualities. Too often, perspectives on gender carry alarmingly dogmatic projections which blur the issues and serve only to entrench prejudice. Claims like these do need to be questioned rather than just believed, or laughed at (my original response). This is not just because of the insulting and patronizing position they take up in relation to homosexual and transgendered people, but also because they genuinely do make it difficult for the rest of us to see the wood from the trees.

In this sense, perhaps the most important thing about this book is that it clearly illuminates how the question of gender goes way beyond whether one feels comfortable in one's own skin as man, woman, feminine, masculine, heterosexual, homosexual, etc. - important though that undoubtedly is. This of course is not new, but the book does convey well the way in which gender-related issues reach right to the heart of our deepest origins and also deeply influence whole ways of thinking about the world - ways which can be narcissistically restrictive and repetitive or ways which can be productive and liberating.

It is interesting that Leslie Murdin has entitled her paper The Future of the Transference-Based Therapies. It conveys a feeling that the debates about research into psychotherapy present some kind of fundamental threat to the future of these therapies, and this message continues throughout her paper. As she describes recent political and institutional developments around IAPT her misgivings are understandable (although her characterization of cognitive-behavioural therapy [CBT] as a ‘mechanical means’ to a quick cure is perhaps a little extreme). Are depression sufferers to be given short shrift as part of a government economic panic to get them back into employment? May a flood of new CBT workers ease other talking therapies out of the NHS? But as she goes on to locate the origins of this policy in some kind of general research-endorsing perspective (instead of merely in specific proposals emanating from certain political subgroups), we are encouraged to become ever more afraid of something which should be our ally, namely information about when our work succeeds, and when it fails to help people feel better, that is, better about the things for which they sought therapeutic help. I feel her anxiety needs tempering and, in responding, I will adopt a stance of cautious optimism that within the coming decade psychodynamic (transference-based) work will become increasingly accepted, despite the pessimism evinced by not only Murdin herself but many of our professional colleagues. There are two broad reasons for my sanguine outlook, one the nature of the issue and the accumulating evidence, the second the changes that have recently been taking place in public opinion and institutions about what can be permitted to count as evidence of therapeutic help.

Elizabeth O'Loughlin  

In time-honoured tradition, this collection of papers reflects something of the extraordinary nature of psychoanalytic thinking and its therapeutic potential. It also explores the nature of its role, position and standing within the wider therapeutic community. We start with Jean Knox, who rises robustly to the challenge reflected by recent research into the necessary conditions for diversity within psychoanalytic thinking to become a factor of creativity and progress (Jimenez 2008). The author continues her published work in this area, focusing on the need for a broader, more integrated vision of what constitutes, contributes to and facilitates ‘the analytic relationship’. Identifying the way in which each of the traditional psychoanalytic and Jungian models has effectively concentrated on differing rather than mutually exclusive aspects of the psyche and its process, she lays the groundwork for a rich drawing together in her paper. Within this are not only these different traditions, but also their newer North American relational counterpart, as well as divergent neuroscientific, developmental and attachment theory perspectives. The article illustrates, with the aid of a cross-paradigm grid and clinical vignettes, how all these can work together concurrently and even simultaneously, enriching each other in the fostering of a creative developmental process within the analytic dyad. Challenging us to question the security of our own chosen theoretical positions, in favour of more creative and inclusive discourses, the paper illuminates the way in which false divisions and political demarcations may have come to limit our overall vision of the psychotherapeutic endeavour.

The next four papers take up, among other things and in differing ways, the question of the father. In his beautiful paper, ‘Family Romances’, Freud quotes the old legal tag: ‘“pater semper incertus est” [paternity is always uncertain], while the mother is “certissima” [certain]’ (1909, p. 239). This question of the meaning, position and significance of the father was one which preoccupied Freud throughout his life, and it has been raised, addressed and raised again in the years since his death.

Attachment & Human Development9(2), 95-109, 2007

How Affect Regulation Moderates the Association between Anxious Attachment and Neuroticism

Thomas N. Crawford, Phillip R. Shaver and H. Hill Goldsmith

Correlations between anxious attachment and neuroticism (usually about 0.40 to 0.50) prompt questions about whether self-reported anxious attachment captures a key construct in attachment theory or if it reflects a more general personality trait instead. A college sample of late adolescents and young adults (N = 287) was used to show that questionnaire measures of neuroticism and anxious attachment do not have a simple linear association; instead, neuroticism and anxious attachment have a more complex dynamic relationship that is moderated by avoidant attachment, an attachment style that reflects an interpersonally derived strategy for affect regulation. The association between neuroticism and anxious attachment is further moderated by conscientiousness, a personality trait that may reflect a more biologically mediated system of affect regulation. These separate moderating effects and the different affect regulation systems they reflect are discussed in the context of long-standing debates about how personality traits and attachment styles influence each other.



Attachment & Human Development9(4), 343-353, 2007

John Bowlby and Couple Psychotherapy

Christopher Clulow

The centenary of John Bowlby's birth provides a context for considering the policy, research and practice legacies that he left for practitioners working in many different fields supporting couples and families. Part historical, and part forward-looking, this paper considers the links between attachment in the infant-parent dyad that was at the heart of Bowlby's concern and the nature of the affective ties that bind couples together in adult romantic relationships. An overview of the influence of his theory on family policy and adult attachment research is followed by an appreciation of its significance for the practice of couple psychotherapy. The paper concludes with a comment on the implications of current neuroscience knowledge for therapeutic technique.

Response to ‘the Future of the Transference-Based Therapies’

Georgia Lepper PHD

Georgia Lepper

[g.lepper@kent.ac.uk]

Georgia Lepper  

Lesley Murdin's paper starts from the presumption that clinicians, and researchers too, are concerned with fostering the development of good psychotherapy practice, and the delivery of better treatments to patients, and indeed the ethical imperative to do so. The paper sets out to address ‘the meaning of the requirement for an evidence base that emanates from the NHS and the universities’. In this response, I propose to examine some questions which arise from the issues raised in the paper. What is ‘evidence’ and how does it relate to the term ‘evidence base?’ What is ‘required’? What does ‘research’ do, and does it have anything to offer the clinician? I will then apply the ‘findings’ of my enquiry to the research cited in Murdin's paper, which is reported in the article ‘Comprehensive process analysis of insight events in cognitive-behavioural and psychodynamic-interpersonal psychotherapy’ by Elliott et al. (1994).

What is Evidence, and How Does it Become an ‘Evidence Base’?

Evidence is a multifaceted term which may be used in philosophical, judicial or scientific contexts. What it shares in all these contexts is the notion that it relates what is observed or discovered to the understanding of what is observed. Evidence is the foundation stone of systematic enquiry, whether philosophical, judicial or scientific: what do our observations/discoveries tell us about the nature of the experienced world, the object of enquiry? Questions then arise: what counts as evidence? How can it be verified, or falsified, as supporting a theory? What part does ‘interpretation’ play in the evaluation of evidence? These are on-going questions for scientific method and are articulated in a variety of forms, as new methods evolve and enquiry deepens. The discussion of the ‘Comprehensive Process Analysis’ method below shows how one method evolved to address some of these questions.

What, then, is an ‘evidence base’? Used popularly, as it is in this paper, it refers to the very recent phenomenon of ‘evidence-based medicine’.

Estela Welldon, feminism, criminal justice system, ‘good womanhood’, violence against women, law-psychiatry interface

In this article the author, a human rights lawyer, pays tribute to the influence that Estela Welldon's work has had beyond the consulting room. Contrary to the prevailing view held in society as a whole, and particularly propounded by feminists who viewed women's abusive behaviour only within the context of a patriarchal society, Welldon's views helped her to understand women's violent and perverse behaviour. The article outlines some ways in which legislation concerning crimes committed both against and by women has changed in the last 20 years. However, mythologies around ‘good womanhood’ which permeate decision-making still abound. The article notes areas in which society's attitude to women is still prejudicial.

Janine Sternberg and Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

The articles in this edition of the BJP form a record of the conference that was held in May 2008 to mark the twentieth anniversary of the publication of Mother, Madonna, Whore: The Idealization and Denigration of Motherhood, and to celebrate the work of Dr Estela Welldon. Mother, Madonna, Whore is so much a part of the clinical landscape now, along with Welldon's conceptualization of perverse mothering, that it is hard to picture a time when the book did not exist. Yet as Welldon has recently written, recalling the 1980s, ‘I was completely new and my work unknown’ (Welldon 2008).1 In this sense the Journal provides not only a record of an event - the conference - but a survey of a clinical and cultural debate as it took shape and evolved. As will be apparent from the articles, Estela Welldon has not only been immensely influential in the field of forensic psychotherapy, groundbreaking in her recognition of female violence and perversion and an inspiration to those involved in group psychotherapy; she is also clearly held in great personal esteem. One of the features which distinguishes her is an unstinting appreciation of the contributions of others, and many of the articles emphasize her warmth and dynamism. We hope that these papers, together with her own article which reviews her 40-year career and reflects on the state of forensic psychotherapy now, will give the reader a sense of (almost) having been present on the day.

The conference was put on by the Portman Clinic in London, where Dr Welldon worked for 30 years. As Stan Ruszczynski states in his Introduction, the Portman is an NHS outpatient clinic which offers assessment and psychotherapeutic treatment to children, adolescents and adults, who enact delinquently, criminally or violently, or who act on their sexual impulses in ways which are disturbing or damaging to others or to themselves. Estela Welldon's paper, ‘Dancing With Death’, contextualizes the Portman Clinic's psychodynamic approach to perversion, and situates the development of her own work in relation to, among others, the early influence of Horacio Etchegoyen and Karl Menninger.

Psychotherapy and the ‘Plague’: Some Contributions to the Understanding of A Recurring Threat

Michael Briant

Michael Briant

1 Church Rate Walk, Cambridge CB3 9HJ. [michaelbriant@ntlworld.com]

Michael Briant  

authoritarian, humiliation, conscience, humanistic, inequality, shame, homophobia, violence

Violence perpetrated in the name of religious or moral regeneration is neither new nor peculiar to any particular creed or ideology. It is an ancient phenomenon, the history and psychology of which have been extensively studied, especially in Northern and Central Europe.

The paper considers a case history of one major manifestation of it in the twentieth century, and related attempts to conceptualize key problems it raises. A link is made with the more recent research of James Gilligan, a leading modern theorist of violence. This wider perspective is needed if we are to understand and combat the re-emergence of the phenomenon today.

Psychotherapy and Research: A Relation That Needs to Be Reinvented

Stijn Vanheule PHD

Stijn Vanheule

[stijn.vanheule@ugent.be] [http://www.psychoanalysis.ugent.be/]

Stijn Vanheule  

randomized controlled trials, evidence-based practice, empirically supported therapies, effectiveness, efficacy, psychotherapy research, psychoanalysis, psychodynamic psychotherapy

In this paper I question whether the randomized controlled trial (RCT) and the evidence-based medicine model are well suited for psychotherapy research. First I discuss general characteristics of the randomized controlled trial and argue that, given a number of incompatibilities with the discipline of psychotherapy, these trials tend to provide us with data that have limited validity. The methodological objections I raise are important as the treatment protocols produced within the context of randomized controlled trials tend to be forced upon clinical practice in uncritical ways. On the other hand, I argue that systematic research is relevant for psychotherapy. If research is designed to address concerns arising from clinical practice - in particular, the far-reaching complexity of the therapeutic encounter - it can be a powerful tool for further developing our discipline.

Peter Wilson

Peter Wilson

London
[peterjbwilson@btinternet.com]

Peter Wilson  

‘I shall not first give an historical survey and show the development of my ideas from the theories of others … What happens is that I gather this and that, here and there, settle down to clinical experience, form my own theories and then, last of all, interest myself in looking to see where I stole what’ (p. 146; Winnicott 1945). This is not untypical of Winnicott. He often writes simply and honestly. We keep on quoting him. He enlivens our talks and lectures when tedium threatens. Of course he read the theories of others, not least Freud, but it as if he were saying here that he did not feel duty bound by them or fettered by the institutions that housed them. It may well be that in the very ordinariness of a remark such as this resides the clue to Winnicott's originality, born of playfulness.

In many ways, what Winnicott had to say was clear and memorable. However, he was not always easy to follow. As Martin James wrote in a letter to Winnicott in 1961, there was a ‘mixture of fright and misunderstanding [surrounding] your work in some circles. Those with literal or obsessional minded approaches cannot comprehend your allusive and illustrative skills, which I find so attractive’ (p. 165; Rodman 2003). There are certainly many times when Winnicott's meaning is difficult to catch hold of. One thought or other slides imperceptibly into another thought or other. The ground often seems to shift and it can all be a little bit infuriating - but at the same time, it is always compelling. We can't leave it be.

This is another book that can't leave Winnicott be - but it is by no means one book too many. It is collection of chapters by a range of experienced psychoanalysts who have been associated in different ways with his work. One of the reasons for Winnicott's sometimes obscure writing was the obscurity of what he was trying to examine. The nature of the early mother/baby relationship, of the intricacies of the psychoanalytic process, of the formation of the child's personality, of the creativity of play were just some of the subjects under his scrutiny. None of these subjects could draw forth conclusions with precise definition - and they are open for further elaboration as in this book.

Patricia Polledri  

This book has been written by forensic psychotherapists whose concern it is to develop a psychodynamic understanding of the offender patient and, in this context, the crime becomes the means of a behavioural enactment by the patient, which uniquely demonstrates something of their internal object relations.

The psychotherapy of those with criminal tendencies and a history of catastrophically dangerous behaviour has its historical roots in this country in the appointment of visiting psychotherapists to the prisons under the auspices of the Home Office. This practice goes back prior to World War II and to the setting up of the Portman Clinic in 1931. This formed the clinical wing of the Institute for the Study and Treatment of Delinquency and was co-founded by Edward Glover, who was a pioneer in the combined field of psychotherapy and criminology.

Emotionally, the horror of murder is one of the most perplexing and chilling subjects to think about, and some of the chapters in this book need close and careful reading and reflection - as neither a socio-political, psychodynamic, nor psychiatric perspective alone can provide any conceptual basis for understanding the aetiology of violence and murder.

The aim of this series is an attempt to understand the origins of murder, as well as describing the highly complex reactions the treatment process generates in both patient and therapist.

The editor explores the history of murder using the concept of Hyatt-Williams's (1998) death constellation - a split-off and encapsulated mental structure that attacks life, when it is triggered by external stressors, breaking loose from its cordon and likely to end in homicidal or suicidal behaviour, or both.

Anthony Cantle

Anthony Cantle

London

Anthony Cantle  

During a recent transmission of a television health programme concerned with the perils of smoking, a sixty-a-day smoker was asked what steps she had taken to give up her habit. She listed all the usual ones she had tried and specifically mentioned that she knew that her local health centre offered a quit smoking group run by one of the nurses but added that she would never go near it. When it was suggested she might not have done so out of embarrassment, her riposte was to make clear that she knew the nurse concerned was ‘a picture of health and had never had a fag in her life and how could someone like that ever know the misery of addiction and the struggle to overcome it’.

This is not a charge that can be levelled against Denise Cullington whose very refreshing book Breaking Up Blues draws thoughtfully but appropriately upon the painful, yet ultimately illuminating experience of her own divorce and manages to do so in a way that avoids the wearisome pitfalls of an account full of wounded invective and poorly disguised narcissistic narrative. Instead she brings to her writing a winning amalgam of personal reflection, high-calibre expertise and plain English, jargon-free elaboration of her book's central purpose - the promotion and achievement of survival and growth out of one of life's most challenging and frequently miserable experiences. Within its pages we see the fruits of her training as a clinical psychologist and the development of her skills and personal learning at the Tavistock Clinic and her current work as a psychoanalyst in Oxford.

Her plea for a measure of psychological-mindedness at a time when thinking is usually the first casualty of a messy relationship breakdown is underpinned throughout this impressive book by an understanding that draws upon her personal experience as a wife and mother, together with her years of experience as a gifted clinician working with individuals and couples as they struggle to face and work through the cruelty, injustices and heart-aches that often accompany the deep sense of loss and humiliation of a failed relationship.

Anne Zachary  

This practical little handbook about working with dangerous and violent patients, including those who have killed, addresses a most particular area of work. It focuses on the problem of the feelings engendered in clinicians by such a difficult patient group and how to manage those feelings. It is a book that focuses on countertransference, recognizing it, processing it and then making use of it. Without this facility there would be, as sadly there have been in the past, many more casualties and disasters, repeating of trauma and professional indiscretions. Working with these patients can be dangerous and the close following and awareness of countertransference is the best protection. The patient and staff groups described come from our high secure and medium secure hospitals.

The book begins with a Foreword by Brett Kahr that, using historical examples, acknowledges the dangers. However, I found his argument over-optimistic and curiously circular. He reminds us that forensic psychoanalytic psychotherapy is not new and that (by another name) it predates the foundation of the Portman Clinic, the NHS clinic that first offered teaching in this field. Citing Freud, Marie Bonaparte, Melanie Klein and others who were concerned about violence and criminality in our culture, he goes on to give a comprehensive account of how the field has developed and concludes that there is a growing body of expertise which could, in time, eradicate serious criminality. This over-optimism is not helpful.

Hinshelwood's Foreword then brings us back to something more grounded. He welcomes this volume which acknowledges the human problems of caring for those who are dangerous but not before ‘fastening his seat-belt’, for, as he says: ‘There are people so desperate that they are willing to commit terrible crimes to get their message across and there are carers so assaulted that they must put safety before care’ (p. xix). I am not sure that those committing the crimes have as much choice as he implies. This said, he pays tribute to the fortitude of the human spirit in general and of mental health workers in particular. Addressing the emotional bearing of the intolerable, he writes: ‘We could say, as I think this book does, that the most useful vaccination against madness is to create meanings in its place. And the book goes further to say that the best of vaccines is the creation of shared meanings: meanings shared by the carer and the cared for. As a result the notion of reflective practice is at the centre of this book’ (p. xxi).

Mary Campbell  

On first impression Dr Peter Shoenberg's book on psychosomatic medicine comes across as a kind of text-book divided into sections covering four main areas. The first chapters include the origin of the term ‘psychosomatic’, its history and development, a review of the current body of knowledge relating to stress and the body, and a list and description of the uses of various forms of psychotherapy. These include psychoanalytic, psychodynamic, supportive and cognitive-behavioural therapy, which are the therapeutic treatments most commonly used to treat people with the various psychosomatic disorders. The final chapter entitled ‘Developing a Psychosomatic Imagination’ makes a plea for imaginative and flexible thinking from clinicians in both the medical and psychotherapeutic world in this complex area of disturbance and illness.

In his introductory chapter, Dr Shoenberg defines psychosomatic illness as: ‘any physical illness in which psychological factors have played a significant role in its precipitation and maintenance, and in some cases, in its causation as well’ (p. 6).

International Forum of Psychoanalysis17, 71-81, 2008

‘Objects’ and ‘Characters’ in Psychoanalytical Texts/Dialogues

Antonino Ferro and Giovanni Foresti

The authors propose the use of the narratological category of ‘character’ in psychoanalysis. They consider this notion useful in studying clinical material because it may help in making clearer the distinction between the clinical development of dialogue and the theoretical options that can be used to conceptualize the interaction. In order to facilitate theoretical comparison and effective technical integration, the authors outline three main schemes commonly found in different psychoanalytic traditions: (a) the models with a strong bias toward a reality-oriented approach, which could be defined ‘individual-historical’; (b) the models focused on the patient's internal world, which will be defined as ‘individual-phantasmatic’; and (c) the models centered on the study of the intersubjective clinical facts and usually referred to as theories of the ‘bipersonal psychoanalytic field’. The hypothesis developed in the paper is that the characters of the psychoanalytic materials are to be considered both as a part of a text, which is endowed with a certain stability in the patient's inner world, and as a component of a dialogue that is prone to living dialectical exchanges and transformations.



International Forum of Psychoanalysis17, 91-103, 2008

The Function of the Analyst's Boundaries in the Psychoanalytic Relationship

Barbara Piovano

Two definitions of the concept of analytic boundaries - the analyst's boundaries in the analytic relationship and the boundary between analyst and patient - focus, respectively, on the analytic function and the analytic relationship. A long analysis of a 20 year-old girl is characterized by the analytic work being slowed down by her chronic tendency to arrive late. A miscarriage very early in her pregnancy, occurring almost at the end of the analysis, produces associations and fantasies on ‘crushed’ fetuses and children. It also encourages reflection on the importance of the analytic space, equated by the analyst with the womb, in fostering the development of fetal aspects of the self that do not develop. In the clinical material from two sessions four months before termination, two analytic events - the introduction in the analytic field of the character of the autistic child and the episode of self-disclosure - mark a turning point in the analytic process. In the discussion, the author demonstrates the creative and mutative effects of alterations in technique and style of working, changes that might be seen as a breach of her analytic boundaries and a transgression in relation to her theoretical frame of reference.

Editorial

Elizabeth O'Loughlin and Caroline Hallett

Caroline Hallett

[elizaariadne@blueyonder.co.uk]

[horakhallett@onetel.com]

Caroline Hallett  

In keeping with our wish to publish papers from a diversity of psychoanalytic perspectives, this issue contains a paper from the Lacanian school as well as an introduction to the life and works of Françoise Dolto, the French psychoanalyst, whose work, particularly with children, is strangely absent from the English language. We continue the debate over state regulation by taking up again the vexed question of ‘evidenced-based therapies’ in the form of a short paper and four discussants who respond in very different ways to the concerns outlined in the paper. Such concerns relating to the question of regulation of the profession have been voiced for some time now - see a letter in BJP 20(4) from Haya Oakley in the summer of 2004. The part played by the transference in the training of students of psychoanalysis or psychoanalytic psychotherapy is another subject that seems to have attracted little investigation so we are pleased to present a paper on the importance of the role played by interpersonal dynamics in the teaching process. Finally, we have a paper that revisits the enigmatic work of Bion and Meltzer this time as a means by which to encourage us as practitioners to consider the spirit in which we undertake the complex task of psychoanalysis.

Susan Schwartz's paper gives us a remarkably clear and concise account of the recent thinking and research coming from the Lacanian school of Psychoanalysis in relation to the concept of Ordinary Psychosis. This development she suggests is a response to the change in the nature of the social link between people which can lead to an increase in symptoms, particularly the addictions that need no one else to produce satisfaction. She tracks clearly the complex development of Lacan's thesis on psychosis that is organized around the mechanism of ‘foreclosure’. Schwartz outlines Lacan's early work when he made his radical suggestion that the analyst needs to occupy the position of ‘secretary’ to the psychotic patient, through to his later work when he used the writings of James Joyce to illustrate the means of knotting the three registers of psychic experience: the Real, Symbolic and Imaginary.

Much demonology has grown up round the acronym IAPT. This paper considers the current state of its effect on the discipline in which we practise. Faye Carey

Faye Carey

London
[fayefree@dsl.pipex.com]

Faye Carey  

The central theme of Freud's Art: Psychoanalysis Retold appears to be that just as the process of analytic listening has the potential to render meaningful for the patient what was chaotic, so may ‘taking in with our eyes what we see in the artist's art’ (p. 120) have the capacity to effect similar internal transformations. Janet Sayers sets out to retell the story of psychoanalysis through art - either as an art in its own terms, or through art's professed affinity with the aims, processes and manifestations of psychoanalysis. Sayers's retelling takes the form of describing through single chapters aspects of the work of ten analysts and two art critics, and their varying approaches to the ‘art’ of psychoanalysis, with each chapter alluding to aspects of art - mainly visual - as may be referenced, or relevant to, the theory and practice of psychoanalysis. There is, however, no clear overriding theory - of either art or psychoanalysis - around which these ideas coalesce, so the work comes across more as a patchwork held together by their common themes but one whose separate squares are stitched together from irregular colours, textures and shapes brought together to constitute the final lively and interesting, if somewhat uneven, quilt.

The book's title introduces an ambiguity that persists throughout, ‘Freud's Art’ being both a reference to the art of psychoanalysis, as well as to Freud's abiding interest in the role of art: psychologically, within the culture, certainly, but also his preoccupation with the psyche of the artist, with regard both to Freud's theories of the neuroses, as well as to the genesis of creativity. Sayers introduces her subject by remarking that the histories of modern art and psychoanalysis have often coincided - having in fact grown up more or less side by side this would be inevitable - and notes that Freud's first meeting with Jung, and Picasso's painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon following his decisive encounter with African masks, both took place in the same year, 1907.

Robert Snell

Robert Snell

London
[r.snell@sussex.ac.uk]

Robert Snell  

In a telling passage towards the end of Generation, Jean White reflects on the omnipotence inherent in any attempt to synthesize psychoanalytic paradigms, especially paradigms as diverse and influential as the three she has invited us to consider in her book: the Independent, Winnicottian tradition, the Lacanian, and the post-Kleinian. For Independents, to seek such a synthesis would be to refuse ‘the bracing developmental shock of a confrontation

408

with external difference’; for Lacanians it would mean staying caught up in the ‘Imaginary’, the illusion that reality can be made to conform to one's own narcissistic image. It would also be psychotic. Post-Kleinians, from their distinctive standpoint, would agree: it would be proof of an inability to adopt different perspectives, to engage with Bion's ‘multiple vertices’ in favour of a delusional state of single-minded certainty. White cites Lacan: ‘… there is no Other of the Other’. Authentic engagement with symbolic meaning involves accepting the absolute otherness of the Other and, bearing one's own lack, the inevitable partiality of one's vision.

The passage is telling on several levels. It exemplifies the reflective quality of White's thinking; it is evidence of a critical agility founded not just in an intellectual grasp of complex theory, but also in the author's feel for the particular theoretical and cultural idiom, the elusive emotional atmosphere, of each of the post-Freudian traditions she addresses. Above all, it underlines the central purpose of her project: far from an attempt at synthesis, her book is an extended argument for analytic pluralism, something not just desirable, but mandatory. For:

The capacity to hold in mind or consider a variety of perspectives at the same time constitutes, in and of itself, a therapeutic instrument of equivalent significance to … the notion of deep containment … the ability to think pluralistically, without forced synthesis, is one of the most potent weapons against ideological fundamentalism … More abuses have been perpetrated in the name of being ‘right’ than ever with knowing maleficence … Pluralistic thinking and the ability to shift perspective are indissoluble from the process of psychoanalytic psychotherapy itself. (p. 13)

Does Intergenerational Transmission of Trauma Skip a Generation? No Meta-Analytic Evidence for Tertiary Traumatization with Third Generation of Holocaust Survivors

Abraham Sagi-Schwartz, Marinus H. van IJzendoorn and Marian J. Bakermans-Kranenburg

In a series of meta-analyses with the second generation of Holocaust survivors, no evidence for secondary traumatization was found (Van IJzendoorn, Bakermans-Kranenburg & Sagi-Schwartz, 2003). With regard to third generation traumatization, various reports suggest the presence of intergenerational transmission of trauma. Some scholars argue that intergenerational transmission of trauma might skip a generation. Therefore, we focus in this study on the transmission of trauma to the third generation offspring (the grandchildren) of the first generation's traumatic Holocaust experiences (referred to as ‘tertiary traumatization’), and we present a narrative review of the pertinent studies. Meta-analytic results of 13 non-clinical samples involving 1012 participants showed no evidence for tertiary traumatization in Holocaust survivor families. Our previous meta-analytic study on secondary traumatization and the present one on third generation's psychological consequences of the Holocaust indicate a remarkable resilience of profoundly traumatized survivors in their (grand-)parental roles.



International Forum of Psychoanalysis17, 16-26, 2008

Feeble Therapies Desperately Seeking Fickle Pathologies

Roland Gori

Medicine, psychology, and psychiatry are not only modes of scientific knowledge or professional practice, but also means of social control that participate in regulating behavior. The ‘re-pathologizing’ of psychiatry during the past 25 years bears witness to an anthropological mutation that reduces the human being to the sum of his or her conduct. In order to get to this ‘medico-economic’ civilization of the subject, post-modern psychiatry has needed to deconstruct and reconstruct its normative landscape for the benefit of ‘fickle’ notions and ‘behavioral disorders’, at the expense of the concept of ‘psychological suffering’.

Ward community groups have been mostly lost from acute psychiatric in-patient settings in recent years with changes related to care in the community and altered therapeutic expectations. Margaret Cohen

Margaret Cohen

Margaret Cohen  

What Can The Matter Be? is part of the rich harvest that springs from the union of Kleinian theory and the infant observation work pioneered by Mrs Bick, which has been the inspiration of the child psychotherapy training at the Tavistock Clinic for over 50 years. The book chronicles the work with under 5s that emerged in the late 1970s and was given form in the Under Fives Service, and was one of the many specialities that grew under the umbrella of that training. What marks the book is the close attention to detail which all the clinicians display, together with their capacity to hold onto their observations in the face of their own uncertainty, until they can use them to elucidate the child's behaviour and the dynamics within the family. This is very much done in the service of the child and of helping the family to find its way forward freed from some unconscious issue by which they have been held up. This often involves helping parents to be in contact with their knowledge of their own infantile experience which then enables them to receive and accept their baby's experience. The book is a breath of fresh air in a culture that has become obsessed with ‘how to do’ books, which hand out advice with little attention to the impact on the child's internal life or the ensuing development of the family.

It is fitting that such a book opens with a paper by Isca Wittenberg who has taught generations of child psychotherapists, both at the Tavistock Clinic and indeed throughout the world. Her baby observation seminars were, as I can vouchsafe, and I imagine still are, an eye-opening experience. One was encouraged to learn to observe in detail, to retain and write this up, to notice when observation became difficult and one's mind left the scene and to face the difficult and often unwelcome aspects of infantile experience both internally and externally. The clinical work in her chapter is based on observation which allows us to understand more about the needs of infants and young children as well as those of the adults looking after them. The discipline of observation is an excellent training for clinical work as it teaches us not to act out, not to do, but to stay with thought and feeling and to remain in an interpretive role. In the heat of work with babies and young children it can be very enticing to act, thereby depriving the families of their chance to internalize a containing experience.

Patricia Polledri

Patricia Polledri

London

Patricia Polledri  

Priscilla Roth, training and supervising analyst at the British Psychoanalytic Institute, and Alessandra Lemma, consultant clinical psychologist at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust, have collected together papers by 14 highly regarded psychoanalysts who have all been inspired, in their own way, to explore, examine and expand on Melanie Klein's theory of envy. They ‘illustrate the rich ideas of key psychoanalysts from the northern hemisphere’ (p. xvii) with their thoughts, hypotheses, opinions and conclusions in relation to the psychodynamics of working with envious experiences.

The book joins Karnac's Psychoanalytic Ideas and Applications series, the aim of which is to focus on the production of significant authors whose works are of outstanding value to the development of the field of psychoanalysis. In this context, Klein's object-relations theory decisively marked the transition from classical to present-day psychodynamic research. Her fundamental contribution was to develop a new conception of endopsychic structure. Before Klein, the human psyche was regarded as an apparatus for experiencing and controlling biological instincts originating outside the ego; after Klein, it became possible to see the human psyche as an internal world of a fully personal nature, a world of internalized ego-object relationships, which, partly realistically and partly in highly distorted ways, reproduced the ego's relationships to personal objects in the real, outer world.

This paper takes Bion's question ‘What sort of artists can we be?’ and begins the quest for an answer. In the light of the later aesthetic model posited by Bion and Meltzer, I consider first the nature and properties of symbols as containers for meaning, then the problem of how symbols are formed and metabolized by means of the transference-countertransference. Finally attention is drawn to the musical resonances of the ‘countertransference dream’ which have traditionally been overshadowed by verbal and visual considerations.

The Testes: Theoretical Lacunae and Clinical Imperatives

Gary Winship PHD MA RMN DIP GP PSYCH CERT ADD

Gary Winship

Wollaton Road, Nottingham NG8 1BB. [Gary.Winship@Nottingham.ac.uk] [www.winship.info]

Gary Winship  

testes, object relations, psychotherapy

In locating the testicles on the object relations map, their function (actual and symbolic) in Sophocles' three plays (Oedipus the King, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone), is considered as a basis for a theory of the testes as transgenerational containers of pathology. Two clinical vignettes are presented where the testes were salient in the course of psychoanalytic psychotherapy; firstly, in the treatment of a manic depressive patient who had developed testicular cancer after the birth of his son, and secondly, in a male patient with gender dysphoria who was seen for psychotherapy prior to operative gender re-assignment. It is argued that the psychobiological role of the testicles has been largely overlooked in psychoanalytic theory. Implications for future consideration of the testes are considered.

‘Forensic Group Psychotherapy’: Estela Welldon's Contribution to Working with Groups at the Portman Clinic

AZ Hakeem MB BS MRCPSYCH

AZ Hakeem

8 Fitzjohns Avenue, London NW3 5NA. [website: http://www.drazhakeem.com] [email: az@drazhakeem.com]

AZ Hakeem  

Estela Welldon, forensic psychotherapy, sexual perversion, delinquency, group psychotherapy, group analysis

In this paper the author gives a summary of the contributions made by Dr Estela Welldon to the Group Psychotherapy at The Portman Clinic. He describes how clinicians working at the Portman Clinic have evolved and adapted the principles and practices from group psychotherapy in order to work with perverse, violent, delinquent, transsexual and other specialist patient groups in what is described as ‘forensic group psychotherapy’. Attention is drawn to the selection of patients, composition of the group, particular differences of dynamic administration of the group, the style of the conductor, and the observed and expected group processes. The author describes his personal experience as a specialist registrar in forensic psychotherapy at the Portman Clinic working with Dr Welldon, and his continued work there as a consultant, and the continual development and evolution of forensic group psychotherapy.

Philip Hewitt  

The Anorexic Mind by Marilyn Lawrence is part of the Tavistock Series and an important addition to the literature on anorexia. The author is able to give her work a ‘dual focus’ as she draws on experience from private psychoanalytic practice and work in the hospital setting each with its own advantages and limitations. It is worth emphasizing that Lawrence also writes with a modesty which, in my view, has the effect of giving a steady and thoughtful feel throughout the book. This is one of the qualities that illumines just how powerful are psychoanalytic theories of mind, yet often at their best when just discreetly a part of the therapeutic culture. At the same time Marilyn Lawrence is a psychoanalyst who tells us of her ‘belief in the continuity of life and development in human individuals’ (p. 4). This emerges as axiomatic of the whole book which is a serious scientific clinical work, yet we also we get a deep sense of compassion and understanding of the psychic terrors and controls which support a fortress of resistant symptoms frustrating therapeutic endeavours.

In ‘Historical Perspectives and Contemporary Debates’ (Chapter Two) Lawrence brings to mind the patient who once told me of her ‘awesome experience of starving and so being in control of her own body’.

Beate Schumacher  

Dear Editors

Thank you very much for the opportunity to respond to Anna Motz's letter regarding my paper in BJP 24(3): 317-27.

Estela Welldon's thinking on motherhood has, of course, been hugely important and all those of us working with mothers, whose difficulties have serious consequences for their children, owe an enormous debt to her. However, rather than a detailed discussion of current analytic thinking on perversions of motherhood or female narcissism, the primary aim of this paper was to draw attention to the need for treatments appropriate to this patient group and their children. Clinical examples given in the course of trying to make this case are thus set in the context of recent legal and policy guidance; doing justice to Welldon's work, it seemed to me, would not have been possible within the confines of this endeavour.

This is the third biography of Khan to have been written over the last 20 years. The first was written by one of his ex-patients, Judy Cooper, Speak of Me As I Am: The Life and Work of Masud Khan (Karnac, 1993). There followed Masud Khan: The Myth and The Reality by R. Willoughby (Free Association Books, 2005). Linda Hopkins's decision to write this biography grew out of her respect for his early analytic writing. She was training to become an analyst in Philadelphia and was puzzled as to why he was not widely read or studied in the USA. This biography might be said to be an exploration of this question, for he is acknowledged to have had literary gifts and to have contributed several original ideas in his first three books, The Privacy of the Self (1974), Alienation in the Perversions (1979) and Hidden Selves (1983), yet his writing is seldom referred to in trainings in the UK and the USA. One answer to that question might be found in his last book, When Spring Comes (1988). His description of boundary violations and his extravagant anti-Semitism in the chapter ‘A Dismaying Homosexual’ finally brought him into public disgrace and expulsion from the BPAS though, as Hopkins shows, some believed this expulsion was long overdue.

Hopkins's biography of Masud Khan (1924-1989) took 13 years to write which is not surprising for it is an extensive work with detailed references and notes as well as interviews with many of his colleagues and ex-patients. She charts his slow descent into megalomaniac madness in a way that is reminiscent of the tragedies of Mozart's Don Giovanni and Shakespeare's King Lear, but Khan's self-destructive life does not have the redemptive quality of melody or poetry that leaves the heart uplifted. Instead one is left with the feeling that ‘he had too much rage and not enough courage’ (p. 234), as his friend Robert Stoller wrote after Khan's death.

Psychotherapy and Research: A Relation That Needs to Be Revised

Harold Bourne

Harold Bourne

Via P. de Cristofaro 40, 00136 Roma, Italy
[bourneharold@hotmail.com]

Harold Bourne  

Dear Editors

There is one serious and unfortunately commonplace error in Stijn Vanheule's studious paper in the February issue (BJP 25(1): 91-109). While contending that the Randomised Control Trial (RCT) and the medical research model are grossly unsuited for psychotherapy (and I would add for drugs, ECT, and treatments in general in the mental health field), he takes for granted that they are totally acceptable in clinical medicine. Actually, they are not, being often convincing or suggestive, but occasionally irrelevant or worse. It should be better known that the patient in RCTs is no longer a person but one of 50 or 100 nameless containers of some pathology or other for which a treatment is tried out. Is that good enough? Sometimes, but not always.

For 10 years in Britain, the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) has issued what have become imperatives rather than so-called guidelines for medical treatment, which are indeed based on RCTs but also on what it somehow calculates the NHS can afford in the number of Quality Adjusted Life Years to be gained by whatever new drug. At this point, the NHS doctor only needs, and increasingly uses, a computer in his pocket to decide what treatment a patient should have.

Clinical judgement and experience thus go out of the window even though the day-to-day conditions confronted in medicine, such as high blood pressure, arthritis, asthma, pregnancy, ageing, to mention a few, do not lend themselves to any unitary approach by guidelines.

There are any number of RCTs showing that anti-depressants and ECT are useless, yet clinical experience over fifty years vividly provides the reverse. Meanwhile, NICE has ordained that psychotherapy in the NHS be synonymous with cognitive-behavioural therapy, although in real life it achieves little of consequence and then only briefly.

In sum, I am urging that psychotherapy be recognised as in the same universe as clinical medicine. Vanheule's paper seems to contradict that.

David Morgan  

This brings together a number of seminal papers on psychoanalytic approaches to working with the borderline patient. Each paper is accompanied by an Internet discussion. This discussion happened following the papers being made available to the IJPA Internet discussion group prior to publication. This format was an attempt to provide a debating forum for analysts. Whilst I believe this format will be an enduring part of future debate and will, I am sure, open up the dialogue around psychoanalytic theory, I think it will be important in the future to avoid the tendency for different groups representing diverse approaches to become entrenched in defending their various theoretical positions. This may be an inevitable development but one hopes that, as the Internet medium opens up and becomes more accessible to a wider membership, the contributors are able to develop a greater level of interactive discourse.

The papers in this book also represent very different theoretical ideas from a diverse group of clinicians with a wide range of patients who span borderline pathology from suicidal enactment to attacks on thinking and delusional beliefs about the mind and body. All the papers seek to find ways of overcoming the perennial problem of trying to reach the borderline patient. Fonagy, in his Introduction, defines the term borderline as a combination of profound relationship disturbance, following a chronic fluctuating course, covering a wide range of psychiatric problems that frequently occur together and following a relatively slow and tumultuous treatment process with often quite limited responses to treatment. This definition highlights the difficulty of bringing such a wide spectrum of clinical problems under one diagnostic category and even challenges, in my view, the need to have one over-arching clinical label.

As we see in this book, this exploration of the so-called borderline ranges from dramatic changes in technique with suicidal or violent patients (Bateman), to emphasizing dream interpretation as the royal road to the psychotic part of the patient and the central phobic position (Green), the emotional unconscious as opposed to the dynamic unconscious (De Masi), unconscious delusions that insulate the subject from experience (Caper), and the female use of her body as a repository for the fragile self (Squitieri). All these ideas added something to my work with the borderline patients that I see and it was difficult, as with a lot of new ideas, not to begin to use them to immediate effect.

Alejandro Reyes  

The experience of time is the essence of human existence. It sounds like an idle, metaphysical statement. Yet, on reading this outstanding collection of seven essays we may accept that the basic human conflict addressed by psychoanalysis is the one between the subjective, experiential times, of diverse speeds and directions, and the abstract, linear, objectified, chronological time in which we live socially.

In his theoretical essay, ‘The Construction of Heterochronicity’, André Green offers us a panorama of these experiential times and their role in structuring the mind. He takes us through the development of Freud's notions of time at different stages in his thinking beginning with Studies on Hysteria where fixation is described as a block in the flow of mental time. But Freud does not remain within a linear notion of time, and is already putting forward a ‘structural’ view of time in the notion of trauma as a complex temporal arrangement; in Green's words, ‘trauma is … “filed” in concentric layers of memory crossed by radiated side paths’, suggesting “… a transchronic functioning” … represented from a synchronic perspective of time in psychotherapy' (p. 2, para 1).

Editorial

Caroline Hallett and Hazel Robinson

Hazel Robinson

[challett@talktalk.net]

Hazel Robinson  

The themes of containment, resilience and the search for a mind of one's own link the thought-provoking papers in this issue. From different perspectives these papers invite us to consider the growth of the thinking mind, and the myriad ways in which its presence or absence can be inferred. It is therefore no coincidence that a number of our authors refer to Bion's theories about the development of thought.

Graham Music offers us a refreshingly candid and heartfelt paper, ‘What has psychoanalysis got to do with happiness? Reclaiming the positive in psychoanalytic psychotherapy’, in which he considers the relation of psychoanalysis to happiness. He makes a strong case for counterbalancing the therapeutic value of focusing mainly on the uncovering of painful affects and destructive drives with work on the psyche's more positive and hopeful capacities. He suggests that this change of emphasis fosters the resilience that allows humans to thrive. Drawing on findings from behavioural research and neuroscience, he makes a fundamental distinction between managing unhappiness and experiencing happiness. His thinking is illustrated with two lively case examples, one of a child, the other of an adult patient. Both vividly demonstrate the therapeutic benefit of listening for underlying resilience and optimism which can be reflected back to the patient.

In the next fascinating paper, ‘The body speaks: Bion's protomental system at work’, Richard Morgan-Jones offers a coherent structure within which the encoded communication of the body can be deciphered. Morgan-Jones begins by exploring Bion's concept of ‘protomentality’ and its relation to group disease (Bion 1989, 1991). According to this concept the prototype for the idea of belonging to a larger body is the somatic experience of containment first within the womb and then within ‘the psycho-physical womb of mother's thoughtful care’.

Introduction

Dorothy Hamilton

Dorothy Hamilton

Dorothy Hamilton  

AGIP, the Association for Group and Individual Psychotherapy, has from its inception in 1974 included in its training syllabus the subject ‘Fairy Tale’. Trainees choose a myth, legend or fairy story, and analyse it through the three lenses of Freudian, Kleinian and Jungian theory. This exercise is in line with AGIP's tradition of breadth and inclusivity, in terms not only of the range of psychoanalytical theories taught, but in the attention paid to the overarching metapsychologies of the theorists.

The ‘Fairy Tale’ work, which allows considerable freedom to trainees in the way they choose to present it, produces strong and lasting understandings of aspects of theory and of the minds of the theorists. Still more powerfully, it evokes and illuminates the role of symbol, metaphor and drama through the characters and their interplay, the structure and unfolding of the story itself, and through its deeper underlying meanings. The study turns out to be one not only of theoretical but of clinical illumination: transference and countertransference, emotional response to the other, nuances of meaning in communication, all are here.

These stories by their very endurance bear witness to their wide and universal meaning for humanity. And each trainee has inevitably chosen, wittingly or otherwise - and never with the fuller understanding that later emerges - a story of deep personal significance for him or herself.

Fittingly, our Annual Lecture in 2008 centred on this theme. The chosen myth was that of The Odyssey, that great quest for identity, kinship and truth - and, as Meg Harris Williams (2005) has it, of reunification with one's Muse. The papers given by our two speakers, Jean White and Carol Leader, are presented here. Jean White was invited as our guest speaker. Her paper is written from a contemporary Independent, Lacanian and post-Kleinian perspective, the latter strand influenced by Bion's radical new theories of mind. Carol Leader, an AGIP member, speaks from the Jungian perspective.

Jean White

London
[jeanwhite333@hotmail.com]

Jean White  

In The Evocative Object World, Christopher Bollas reflects on and expands some of the most central preoccupations of his life's work to date. He continually stresses the importance of returning to the original Freudian meaning of the analysand's free association or ‘free talking’ (p. 8), by which he means simply moving freely from topic to topic without ignoring the apparently irrelevant. This, together with its counterpart of the analyst's immersion in her own receptive unconscious, are the fundamental tenets of psychoanalytic practice. Indeed Bollas contends that the principal psychoanalytic objective is to increase the unconscious capacity of both patient and analyst, thereby generating ‘… a new form of creativity fostered only in the psychoanalytical space’ (p. 11). One aim of psychoanalysis is therefore to enhance unconscious communication and tune in to the unconscious thought composed of ‘… multiple lines of psychic interest’ (p. 13). Of equal significance, and working in a dialectical relationship with this enhanced unconscious receptivity, is the openness needed to be played by the objects we select in external reality and even sometimes by those foisted upon us or those that arrive by chance. At best we can allow these objects to enrich the articulation of the deeply unconscious idiom that constitutes ourselves.

The Evocative Object World takes up and further develops some of the themes Bollas began to explore in The Shadow of the Object (1987), continued work on in Forces of Destiny (1989), evolved most intensively in Being

Estela Welldon's analyses of female violence show that we cannot understand any violence, including that of men, without understanding that of women. Past research has identified shame and humiliation as a necessary, but not sufficient, cause of violence. Why, then, are women not more violent than men since they are often treated as inferior to men? Because both sexes are honoured for conforming to the gender role into which they are socialized, and are shamed for behaving in ways assigned to the other sex. Men are honoured for being perpetrators and victims of violence, and hence ‘violence-objects’, and shamed for non-violence. Women, by contrast, are honoured for sexual chastity and non-violence, and shamed for having sex outside marriage, behaving violently, or in any other way behaving like a man. They thus become ‘sex-objects’ (having renounced their sexual subjectivity), and will become violent only if (like Medea), they have already been shamed so severely and irretrievably that they have nothing more to lose by resorting to violence.

Jean Knox PHD MBBS MRCPSYCH

Jean Knox

209 Woodstock Road, Oxford OX2 7AB. [jm.knox@btinternet.com]

Jean Knox  

transference, countertransference, individuation, affect regulation, reflective function, self-agency

This paper highlights some key features of a Jungian approach to transference and countertransference and suggests that a Jungian model has crucial aspects in common with contemporary views in attachment theory on the nature of the analytic relationship. The analytic relationship is examined in terms of the fundamental processes of psychic development described in attachment theory and affective neuroscience, namely affect regulation and development of reflective function and of self-agency. The relative value of three analytic techniques, those of interpretation, new relational experience and regression, are discussed in relation to these processes. I suggest that each of the traditional psychoanalytic and Jungian analytic models concentrates on differing aspects of these psychic processes and analytic techniques. I construct a grid to illustrate this and to demonstrate how attachment theory and developmental neuroscience offer a theoretical basis on which we can develop an integrated model of the nature of the analytic relationship and tasks.

Richard Morgan-Jones  

psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, group dynamics, basic assumptions, protomental, psychosomatic, socio-somatic, organizational dynamics, language of the body, organizational body, mentoring for psychotherapists, health and safety risks for psychotherapists

Psychoanalysis has primarily explored somatic experience in relation to love and intimacy. This paper focuses on the body in relation to work. It explores the experience that what patients increasingly present for analysis are the traumas and pleasures of being caught up with and belonging to a body larger than their own, whether in a couple, a group, a work organization or the body politic. It begins with an exploration of Bion's idea of a relationship between protomentality and group disease. It goes on to consider what can be conceived of as his ecological methodology, which enables movement between different ‘fields of study’ (Bion 1962). These are applied to the health risks encountered by psychotherapists and the profession as a whole. Finally, there is a proposal for mentoring to address professional health, as an under-developed element in the profession.

Carol Leader

Carol Leader

[caroll@freeuk.com]

Carol Leader  

Jung, post-Jungian, individuation, transcendent function, psychoid, archetype, collective unconscious, neuroscience, symbol, alchemy, psychopath, animus, anima, myth, dreams, symmetry, Odysseus, oedipal, Penelope

Homer's epic tale of the 20-year return of Odysseus from the Trojan War is investigated with particular reference to Jung's theory of individuation. Odysseus' meetings with ‘the anima’ in the form of goddesses, sirens and female monsters and his visit to Hades demonstrate the confrontation and humanization of aspects of the archetypal level of the psyche, central to Jung's theories of psychic growth and development. Jung's important ideas of the psychoid level and the transcendent function are explored and linked both to his investigations into medieval alchemy and with findings from contemporary neuroscience. The importance of Jung's constructive method of the interpretation of dreams and myths is shown to be central.

This chapter gives an account of a young woman suffering from a personality disorder who killed her baby and her psychoanalytic psychotherapy treatment in high security over several years. The focus is on three main areas. Firstly, the severity of her family dysfunction, especially her relationship with her own mother, gradually emerged in the course of treatment and this led to the infanticide also being viewed as a suicidal or even matricidal act as the patient's identifications with mother and baby altered repeatedly. Secondly, the course of treatment also raised particular countertransferential difficulties with this patient who was, at times, extremely hostile and occasionally violent during sessions and these are also described. Lastly, prognostic expectations and hopes for patients with this degree of disturbance are reviewed

Jane Bingham

Jane Bingham

[jane@janebingham.plus.com]

Jane Bingham  

religious experience, Anglican priest, spiritual direction, spatio-temporal organization, maternal containment, symbolic father

In qualitative psychoanalytically-informed research the author explores how the internal object-representational world of six stipendiary male Anglican priests might illuminate the psychological significance of their relationship with God. Viewing personality development as a lifelong process permits a more synthetic view of existing theories of God as maternal object, transitional object or oedipal father. A relationship with God may reinforce a good relationship with primary objects, but when failures in maternal containment have resulted in disturbances of the spatio-temporal organization of the infant's mind, new experience - including religious experience - will be superimposed on this distorted psychic substrate. When space-centred thinking dominates, religious objects may offer exogenous structural support to the personality, but in the absence of transformative object relationships they will remain unassimilated. The priestly quest may sometimes be an attempt to establish or repair a triadic internal relationship with a maternal containing object and the symbolic father.

Teaching and Transformation: A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Psychotherapeutic Training

Rosemary Cpsychol AFBPSS

Rosemary Cpsychol

London SW15 4JD. [rosierizq@tiscali.co.uk]

Rosemary Cpsychol  

psychotherapy Training, Psychotherapy Trainees, Unconscious Dynamics, Intersubjectivity, Recognition, Transformation

While there has been much recent interest in the impact of organizational structures underpinning psychotherapeutic training (e.g. Davies 2008; Kernberg 2006), there has been curiously little interest in the impact of interpersonal dynamics on the process of teaching psychotherapy. In this paper, I draw on my experience as a university lecturer and tutor on a postgraduate counselling and psychotherapy training programme to explore some of the unconscious dynamics underpinning the psychotherapy trainee's development towards a mature professional identity. The implicit expectations that trainee psychotherapists hold at the start of their training are initially discussed; I then turn to psychoanalytic writers such as Bollas, Winnicott and Jessica Benjamin in an attempt to articulate and explore how trainees may progress from relating, to constructive use of their tutors in their quest for personal transformation and professional recognition.

Darian Leader

Lesley Murdin's paper poses important questions regarding the future of psychotherapy that no clinician can afford to ignore. There is increasing pressure from both outside the profession and, to a certain extent, from within, to accommodate psychotherapy to the model of a service industry. Therapy becomes an intervention to be locally applied, like a drug, with exactly those features that regulators require of pharmaceuticals: that active ingredients be specified, that the outcomes and benefits be clearly defined and that the time period for delivery of these effects be precise. As Lesley Murdin points out, the framework here is ‘evidence-based research’ (EBR), a slogan that has become almost deafening in those fields that we could call the contemporary pseudo-sciences.

Many psychotherapists feel that they must defend the legitimacy of their profession and have accepted the EBR framework as a gold standard. It is identified with a - sometimes the - scientific approach, with little critique of its practises and conceptual merits. RCTs become the given form in which enquiry is cast, despite the fact that they are totally inappropriate for psychotherapies, for one simple reason: it is not possible to randomize transference. Any model of psychotherapy which recognizes transference will acknowledge that transference is not a variable that can be switched on or off at will, but a basic substructure of all human relationships. Whether it is noisy or discreet, it lays the foundations for all transfers of interest, energy, attachment or belief.

Anorexia Nervosa and the Psychotherapy of Absence

Anthony Winston

Anthony Winston

Lakin Road, Warwick CV34 5BW. [anthony.winston@covwarkpt.nhs.uk]

Anthony Winston  

anorexia nervosa, psychotherapy, object relations, potential space

Absence is characteristic of the psychotherapy of many different types of psychological disorder. However, it is perhaps particularly significant in the psychotherapy of anorexia nervosa. I hope to show that the notion of absence can help to draw together some of the many strands which go to make up this most complex of conditions. Recognition of what is absent can help illuminate the patient's unconscious conflicts and point to the capacities that she has been unable to develop. These absences arise out of early environmental deficiencies, such as a lack of containment, which can result in failures of introjection and an absence of the potential space. They can leave the child ill equipped to experience, understand or deal with her feelings, develop a secure sense of self or think symbolically. Sexual desire, aggression and envy often appear to be absent from the conscious world of the anorexic. In therapy, there is often a striking absence of feeling and of connection between patient and therapist. The work is done largely in relation to what is not talked about, felt or understood and what is apparently not happening. The therapist needs to create a space in which absence and emptiness can be thought about and symbolized, and a sense of self can begin to develop.

Dancing with Death

Estela Welldon MD DSC (HON) FRC PSYCH

Estela Welldon

[estela@evwelldon.com] [www.estelawelldon.org]

Estela Welldon  

perversion, manic defence, faulty mothering, group-analytic psychotherapy, female psychopathology

The author reviews her 40-year professional career in forensic psychotherapy. She describes her formation at medical school in Argentina, the Menninger School of Psychiatry in Topeka, Kansas, and the Henderson Hospital in Surrey. She reflects on her work, for 30 years, at the Portman Clinic. ‘Dancing with death’ is a metaphor for seeking serious danger, and she offers an extensive clinical vignette from her early career to illustrate the complexities involved in the assessment and treatment of perversion, reviewing the case in the light of her more recent thinking. Perversion is seen as a manic defence against the dreaded black hole of depression but, as well as being associated with the death instinct, perversion secures survival. Both features have to be born in mind in therapeutic work, and she considers both technical and transference/countertransference aspects of treatment, emphasizing the particular advantages of group-analytic psychotherapy. The context in which Mother, Madonna, Whore was written is reprised. Lastly, she surveys the work of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy and our developing understanding of severe female psychopathology.

Graham Music

Tavistock Centre, 120 Belsize Park, London NW3 5BA. [gmusic@tavi-port.nhs.uk]

Graham Music  

positive, happiness, resilience, reclamation, psychoanalysis

This paper questions whether what is a strength of psychoanalysis - its focus on painful and difficult experiences and its ability to remain in touch with the negative aspects of the personality - might also be an Achilles heel. The paper discusses research from neuroscience, developmental and social psychology to argue that more attention needs to be given to how we work with more positive and hopeful aspects of the personality, and that otherwise psychoanalytic psychotherapists are not working with the whole person. Some clinical examples are used to illustrate how these ideas might be used.

The Theory of the Basic Assumption of Incohesion: Aggregation/Massification or (BA) I:A/M

Earl Hopper

Earl Hopper

11 Heath Mansions, The Mount, London NW3 6SN. [earlhopper@btinternet.com]

Earl Hopper  

Estela Welldon, the basic assumption of Incohesion: Aggregation/Massification, (ba) I:A/M, traumatogenic processes, annihilation anxiety, crustacean and amoeboid defences/protections, Bion, Foulkes

Presented in honour of Dr Estela Welldon as a friend and colleague, and in acknowledgement of her contributions to forensic psychotherapy and group analysis for people who suffer from extreme anxieties associated with confused sex and gender identifications and choices, sado-masochism and criminality, this article integrates Bionian and Foulkesian perspectives in group analysis by conceptualizing a fourth basic assumption in the unconscious life of social systems. The basic assumption of Incohesion: Aggregation/Massification or (ba) I:A/M is derived from a relational rather than an instinctual metapsychology, and assumes that helplessness and the fear of annihilation precede the emergence of envy, thus emphasizing the importance of traumatogenic processes. Traumatized people with crustacean and amoeboid defences/protections against the fear of annihilation are likely to personify aggregation and massification processes, respectively. This theory can be applied in the group treatments of our most disturbed patients, and in understanding the dynamics of traumatized social systems, ranging from families to organizations and even societies.

The Uses of Humor in Life, Neurosis and in Psychotherapy: Part 1

Zvi Lothane

Joy and sadness, the comic and the tragic, making jokes and telling jokes, have been known in life, literature, the theater, and art since the dawn of civilization. Following in the footsteps of classical antiquity, Freud added to the philosophical analysis of humor the insights offered by the psychoanalytic method. The bridge was the cathartic method of treating neuroses, where discharge of affect was one of the foundations of technique, and the cathartic, or discharge, function of humor. Freud's analysis of humor, that ‘A joke … is the most social of all mental functions that aim at a yield of pleasure’ introduces Freud's first explicit formulation of an interpersonal approach to the human situation in health and disorder.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis89, 299-312, 2008

The Destruction of Time in Pathological Narcissism

Otto F. Kernberg

This paper describes the characteristics of subjective time (in contrast to objective time), with particular reference to a specific form of pathological experience and relation to the passage of time in patients with narcissistic personality undergoing psychoanalytic treatment. The clinical manifestations and technical approach to this pathology of time experience are outlined in the context of illustrative clinical vignettes.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis89, 1123-1143, 2008

‘Caesura’ as Bion's Discourse on Method

Guiseppe Civitarese

The author contends that Caesura, one of Bion's last works, can be read as the equivalent of Descartes's Discourse on Method. In this compact and complex text, the dictate of ‘methodical’ and ‘hyperbolic doubt’ - so called because it is taken to the extreme form of application to the faculty of thought itself - which, for Descartes, represents the fundamental principle of philosophical and scientific research, is reflected in the formula of ‘transcending the caesura’. Bion directs his attention successively to the pairs of opposing concepts that structure psychoanalytic discourse and demonstrates their paradoxical and non-separative logic. The binary system of producing meaning is deconstructed through the systematic use of non-pathological - i.e. not static hut dynamic - reversible perspective. A viewpoint that appears natural, self-evident and primary is plunged into crisis and proves to be founded on what the punctuation mark of the slash excludes. Yet the new point of view does not supplant its predecessor, but supplements it. The conceptual opposition is not overturned, but merely destabilized in such a way as to maintain a creative tension that generates new thoughts. By this technique of wrong-footing the reader, Bion achieves what is tantamount to a Kuhnian revolution: the transition from Freud's semiotic or evidential paradigm to an aesthetic one, centred on emotional experience - to a ‘science of at-one-ment’. Working with the antithetical concepts of censorship and caesura, the author illustrates some clinical implications of this radical shift.

Psychic and Mental Bisexuality in the Development of A Sense of Self and Mind

Judith Hurwood

Judith Hurwood

Leicester LE5 0TA. [judith.hurwood@leicspart.nhs.uk]

Judith Hurwood  

mental bisexuality, psychic bisexuality, self, psychic space, thought, mind, development, containment

Drawing on the ideas of Birksted-Breen (1996) and Houzel (2005), this paper discusses the concept of bisexuality, which has been viewed in various ways in the psychoanalytic literature. An argument is made for a clearer definition and conceptual distinction using the terms ‘psychic’ and ‘mental’ bisexuality. Houzel's ‘psychic bisexuality’ and Birksted-Breen's ‘mental bisexuality’ are distinguished as two separate developmental phases which promote the establishment of psychic space and thought. Psychic bisexuality pertains to the structuring of the self and the development of internal space. Mental bisexuality pertains to the functioning of the mind, with the development of space between internal objects and between self and others. Central to these developments are the containing functions of being both close enough to, and distant enough from, the patient. Clinical material illustrates how interwoven problems at the stage of psychic and mental bisexuality can be and demonstrates that the development of internal space, and space between self and others, requires internalization of both the psychic and mental bisexuality of the therapist.
