Estela Welldon, bodies, female psychology, forensic psychology, motherhood, narcissism, perversion, perverse motherhood, violence

This paper describes how the radical concept of maternal perversion first presented by Estela Welldon (1988) informs the psychotherapeutic assessment and treatment of female inpatients within forensic services and of women in the community who commit acts of violence. It presents a model of the psychology of female violence that the author describes as ‘crimes against the body’. The paper offers clinical evidence for Welldon's model of female perversion in forensic settings and provides an extended clinical illustration of psychotherapeutic work, when the therapist was pregnant, with a woman who killed her child.

A Psychosis More Ordinary: A Lacanian Treatment of Paranoia

Susan Schwartz PHD

Susan Schwartz

[susanschwartz@ozemail.com.au]

Susan Schwartz  

Lacanian treatment of psychosis, Jacques-Alain Miller and ordinary psychosis, untriggered psychosis, paranoia, Borromean knot

Many patients who are diagnosed as borderline within psychiatric discourse are, within the Lacanian orientation, more likely to be considered to have a psychotic structure even though there has been no psychotic break. The concept of ‘ordinary psychosis’ was developed by Jacques-Alain Miller to describe a psychosis that has not been triggered, or has been triggered and has since stabilized. This is not a diagnostic category but rather an epistemic one; it provides a way of thinking about and treating patients who are not clearly neurotic but do not present with any obvious psychotic phenomena.

Comment on ‘“I can't Live without my Child”: Motherhood as A “Solution” to Early Trauma’ by Beate Schumacher

Anna Motz

Anna Motz

[apmotz@aol.com]

Anna Motz  

Dear Editors

I was most surprised not to see any reference to Welldon's pioneering work on perversions of motherhood in Schumacher's recent paper on motherhood as a solution to early trauma (BJP 24(3):317-27). This omission seems most unfortunate as it would have been highly relevant to her discussion and has been influential in shaping contemporary analytic thinking on motherhood and maternal narcissism. I am aware that a forthcoming issue of the British Journal of Psychotherapy is devoted to Welldon's work and its developments, testifying to her enduring influence and making the omission in this paper even more striking.

Yours sincerely

Anna Motz

Trahison Des Clercs: Professional and Political Notes on the Inflation of Psychoanalysis - Responding to Lesley Murdin

Andrew Samuels

Andrew Samuels

148 Mercers Road, London N19 4PX. [www.andrewsamuels.com]

Andrew Samuels  

I want to write this response in a racy and direct manner. The influence of the state and its penetrative bureaucracies has had a bad impact on the way psychotherapists and counsellors think and write. No need only to turn to identification with the aggressor for an explanation, it's more a question of our writing what we think we need to write if we want to be in their gang.

Why does Lesley write about the future of the ‘transference-based’ therapies? Why not the ‘relational’ therapies or some wording that would underscore a difference from what she imagines goes on in CBT. Maybe it is because she is very well informed indeed and knows that those practising dialectical or dialogical CBT also claim that they ‘work with’ the therapy relationship, and so there is a need to up the ante by turning to the unique selling point of psychoanalysis - transference. I suggest we need to see through what is going on in Lesley's paper or any victory we gain will be entirely Pyrrhic.

I have seen much the same process involving a search for what is exceptional in psychoanalysis going on in the meetings held between the former Psychoanalysis and Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Section of UKCP (now the Council for Psychoanalysis and Jungian Analysis) and the British Confederation for Psychotherapy (now the British Psychoanalytic Council). There, some BPC members have announced that what distinguishes psychoanalytic therapies from the others, and placed them in a superior and more demanding category, was that only such therapies work with transference and this, in turn, is because only such therapies have any conception of the unconscious. Hence, the inflated claim continues, work done by the BPC is much more dangerous and demanding than work done by, say, an integrative psychotherapist - which would therefore justify some sort of representation of the hierarchy and differential in any state regulation, whether by the Health Professions Council or another body.

The Psychoanalytic Process by Donald Meltzer. Published by Karnac, London, for the Donald Meltzer and Roland Harris Trust; 109 pp; £19.99.

James Astor

James Astor

London
[james.astor@btinternet.com]

James Astor  

This short book, first published in 1967, sets out in notational form the stages of analysis as understood in the reflective, taking stock, periods after the event. Its intention is to evoke in the professional reader ‘associations to his own experience’. Meltzer conceptualizes the analytic process in metapsychological periods. These conceptualizations come out of application, dedication, hard work, discussion and reflection and are thought of by him as discoveries. Elsewhere he has described imagination as a foraging instinct; here he writes of conceptualization as ‘the capacity to discover beyond the verification’ of what the analyst has been taught. He lists five periods: gathering the transference, sorting geographical confusions, sorting zonal confusions, the threshold of the depressive position and the weaning process. Each of these has distinctive characteristics which he describes occurring within sessions, between sessions and over longer holiday breaks. He calls this the ‘natural history’ of an analysis. The material comes from child analyses.

This book makes use of the hyphenated language of early Kleinian metapsychology (e.g. toilet-breast) which refers to the confusions which exist in part-object relating. One value of this language is that it makes it possible to trace the transformations which occur to these part-objects as they change from being, for instance, a faeces-penis-nipple to becoming a penis-in-a-breast to eventually becoming a breast combined with a nipple, as the move towards the oedipal conflict emerges. But today this language sounds arcane and out of touch with contemporary practice. I will briefly consider the five stages.

‘The Gathering of the Transference’. This refers to the ‘tendency for transference processes to find expression where their anxieties can find relief’ (p. 7). Along with this comes the deepening of the transference in response to the separations of weekend breaks and holidays - separations which are linked to individuation. Meltzer emphasizes that this period of the analysis is ‘where experience counts greatly in relation to time’ (p. 10) as the general improvement that accompanies the ‘gathering of the transference’ ‘is then disrupted by the commencement of patterns of acting out’. This is when the ‘natural history of the analytic process’ ‘takes on a life of its own’ (p. 12).

Dorothy Girouard

Dorothy Girouard

[girouard@dircon.co.uk]

Dorothy Girouard  

Imagine an underground chamber like a cave with a long entrance open to the daylight and as wide as the cave. In this chamber are men who have been prisoners there since they were children … they [are chained so they] can only look straight ahead of them and cannot turn their heads. Some way off, behind and higher up a fire is burning, and between the fire and the prisoners and above them runs a road. In front of which (is) a curtain-wall … like the screen at puppet shows, between the operator and their audience, above which they show their puppets.

There are men carrying all sorts of gear along behind the curtain-wall projecting above it and including figures of men and animals … and some of these men are talking and some are not …

The prisoners [can only see] anything of themselves or their fellows [by] the shadows thrown by the fire on the wall of the cave opposite them…. and … [They assume] the shadows they see (are) the real things. They believe the shadows of the objects … (are) the whole truth.

… Then if [one of them] was released from his bonds and cured of his delusion and forced to stand up … and look and walk towards the fire all these actions would be painful and he would be too dazzled to see properly the objects of which he used to see the shadows…. He would be at a loss and think that what he used to see was far truer than the objects now being pointed out to him.

… And if he were made to look directly at the light of the fire it would hurt his eyes and he would turn back and retreat to the things [the shadows] which he could see properly, which he would think really clearer than the things [now] being pointed out to him.

(Adapted from Plato's ‘The Simile of the Cave’, The Republic, Book VII, Sec. 7)

I begin with this extract from ‘The Simile of the Cave’ (Plato 1984) for it was my entry route into Meltzer's The Apprehension of Beauty. Approximately 2400 years ago Plato saw that man could only face the sun, the ‘eternal truth’, the ‘O’ of Bion's grid, for a moment. He then has to retreat back into the shadowy cave of the paranoid-schizoid position, e.g. the partial perception of the object.
